name: Inside a software factory
intro: For engineers who already use Claude Code: what a software factory is, why verification and the three loops matter, and one real request traced through an eleven-stage pipeline on GitLab.
links: Software Factories: The Next Step in AI Coding Isn't the Cloud (Medium)

scenes.name: Sanjeev Gulati
scenes.line: Building software factories on Claude Code
scenes.say: Sanjeev Gulati · AI Coding Expert
scenes.voice: Hi, I'm Sanjeev. For the last few weeks, I've been building a software factory on top of Claude Code... and running real requests through it.

scenes.title: From agents to a factory
points: Local, remote, and factories: what actually changes.
Autonomy, verification, and the three loops.
The pipeline, the skills, the checker's gates.
From an issue to a merge request.
scenes.voice: In this video, I'll show you how it works. Where it came from, what makes it different from just using agents, what's under the hood... and one real request, from the issue, all the way to a merge request. If you already use Claude Code, this is the next step.

scenes.kicker: For engineers who already use Claude Code
scenes.title:
Inside a software
factory
scenes.say: What changes when you stop driving every session, and build the machine that does it.
scenes.voice: So... you already use Claude Code. Now imagine you stop driving every session yourself, and instead, you build a factory that does it for you. Let me show you what that actually looks like.

scenes.title: Three steps
points: An assistant on your laptop. You prompt, you check every edit, the laptop stays on.
A prompt from the app on your phone or desktop, a browser or Slack. One agent, in a cloud sandbox.
Not where the agent runs: how the work is organised, so it can be trusted to run alone.
scenes.voice: If you look at how AI coding has evolved, it's happened in three steps. It started on your laptop. You prompt, Claude edits, and you check every single change. Then came remote agents. You can open the Claude app on your phone, type a prompt, and it builds in the cloud. And in parallel, something different showed up. Factories. And factories aren't really about where the agent runs... they're about how the work is organised.

scenes.title: Three ways of working
rows: Usually CI runners (GitLab, GitHub Actions); can run from Claude Code on a laptop
A prompt from the app, a browser or Slack; or an issue assigned to it

The agent; some show the plan in the PR

scenes.say: A factory changes who decides, who checks, and what's recorded
scenes.voice: Put them side by side, and here's the thing. Local and remote agents mostly differ in where they run. A factory changes something more important. Who decides what gets built. Who checks it. And what gets recorded. You approve the requirements before anything is built, a separate agent checks the work, and every check leaves evidence behind.

scenes.title: Agents write all the code
scenes.define: A software factory is any agentic system where agents write all of the code you ship. Engineers stop building the product, and build the machine that builds it.
scenes.voice: The definition I like best comes from Dru Knox, at Tessl. A software factory is any agentic system where agents write all of the code you ship. Which means your job changes. You stop building the product... and you start building the machine that builds it.

scenes.title: Autonomy first
points: How often a person has to correct or nudge the agents.
How much can run without anyone reviewing it.
How good the result is for the people who use it.
scenes.voice: So how do you know if your factory is any good? Knox uses three measures, and the order matters. First, autonomy. How often does a person have to step in and nudge the agents? Then automation. How much can you let run without anyone reviewing it? And then quality. You earn automation, by proving autonomy first.

scenes.title: Verification makes it safe
scenes.define: You can stop reading every line only when something else checks it, every time, and leaves evidence you can inspect. Without that, a factory is a faster way to ship mistakes.
scenes.voice: And what makes autonomy safe? Verification. You can only stop reading every line if something else is checking it. Every time. And leaving a record you can actually inspect. Without that, honestly, a factory is just a faster way to ship mistakes.

scenes.title: Three loops
points: Agents iterate before review. Fast and cheap. Raises autonomy.
Thorough checks after the change is up. Replaces review time.
Learns from every correction, and fixes the other two loops.
scenes.voice: Now, a factory runs in three loops. The inner loop is where agents iterate before anything goes up for review. It's fast, and it's cheap. The outer loop is the slower, thorough checking, the kind that replaces your review time. And then there's the meta loop. That one watches the corrections and the failures... and fixes the factory itself, so the same mistake doesn't happen twice.

scenes.title: One pipeline, eleven stages
scenes.key: You: two approvalsAgents: requirements, plan, codeScripts: everything checkable
scenes.say: Eleven stages: agents write, scripts check, a person approves twice
scenes.voice: Okay. Here's the factory I built, on top of Claude Code. It has eleven stages. Agents write the requirements, the plan, and the code. Scripts do everything that can be checked mechanically. And a person steps in exactly twice.

scenes.say: The pipeline is data: who does each stage, and how
scenes.voice: And here's the thing. The whole pipeline is just data. Each stage says who does the work, an agent, a script, or a human, which skill it follows, and what it's allowed to write. If a stage fails three times, the factory stops, and asks a person.

scenes.say: A skill: how one kind of job is done
scenes.voice: Every kind of job has a skill. It's just a short, written instruction. This one's for UI logic. Pure functions, no DOM, no clock. And look at the last line. The maker never ticks its own task, and never writes its own evidence.

scenes.title: One request, start to finish
scenes.say: A CRM dashboard, asked for in plain words on a GitLab issue.
scenes.voice: Alright. Let's watch one real request, go all the way through.

scenes.say: An issue in plain words, labelled for the factory
scenes.voice: It starts as a plain GitLab issue, with the factory label on it. A webhook kicks off a pass, straight away.

scenes.say: The first gate: approve the requirements
scenes.voice: Within about a minute, the requirements are written. And then the factory stops... and waits for a person.

scenes.say: Stories with acceptance criteria every later stage is held to
scenes.voice: The requirements are user stories, with acceptance criteria. Everything downstream gets checked against these, so this approval actually means something.

scenes.say: Approve: one word on the issue
scenes.voice: Approving is one word on the issue. Oh, and no slash. GitLab quietly swallows a comment that's only slash approve.

scenes.say: The plan: sections, skills, and a gate for each
scenes.voice: Next, comes the plan. The work is split into sections, and every section ends with a gate, that the checker has to pass.

scenes.where: the checker's checks, written in the plan
scenes.say: Runnable checks, written before the code
scenes.voice: And these are the checker's gates. They're written into the plan before any code exists. Real commands, with expected results. The module's exports, no DOM access, the currency formatting, totals right down to the cent.

scenes.say: Inner loop: maker builds, a separate checker verifies
scenes.voice: This is the inner loop in action. A maker session builds a section. Then a completely separate checker session, one that never saw the maker work, runs the gate. If it passes, the next section starts. If it fails... a fresh maker gets the written findings.

scenes.say: Evidence: what was run, expected, and found
scenes.voice: The checker writes down its evidence. What it ran, what it expected, and what it actually found. In this run... four sections, four passes, first time.

scenes.say: Outer loop: evidence re-checked, tests, preview
scenes.voice: Then, the outer loop kicks in. A script re-runs the checks instead of trusting them, the full test suite runs, and a preview goes up.

scenes.say: Try it: the real change, running
scenes.voice: Now, the person who asked for it gets to try the real thing, right in a browser. And they approve... again.

scenes.say: A merge request with the specs and evidence
scenes.voice: And then a merge request opens, with the specs and every bit of evidence linked. Merging is still a human's call.

scenes.title: Issue in, merge request out
scenes.key: Nothing on your laptop. Each pass is stateless; its state lives in git.
scenes.say: Webhook, runner, flow.py, claude -p, state in git
scenes.voice: So how does it actually run? An issue or a comment in GitLab fires a webhook, and that starts a pipeline on a runner. Each pass pulls the factory's state from a git branch, walks the stages, and runs claude dash p for every agent step. Then it pushes the work, comments on the issue, and saves its state again. Nothing runs on your laptop.

scenes.title: The loops, made concrete
points: Maker and checker per section; a failed gate goes back with findings, up to three tries.
Evidence re-checked by script, presubmit, preview, then a person tries it.
Every intervention is recorded; fixes go into skills and rules. By hand, for now.
scenes.voice: Mapped back to the loops... the inner loop is maker and checker, per section, with three attempts. The outer loop is scripts and tests, and then a person tries it. And the meta loop? Every time someone has to step in, it's recorded, and the fix goes into a skill or a rule. Honestly... right now, that loop is me. By hand.

scenes.title: Issue to merge request
numbers: issue to merge request, approvals included
sections passed their checker first time
scenes.say: 17 minutes, 10 agent sessions, about $1.24, 4 of 4 first time
scenes.voice: Here are the numbers from that run. Seventeen minutes from issue to merge request, approvals included. Ten agent sessions. About a dollar and twenty cents at API prices. And every single section passed its checker the first time.

scenes.title: What it doesn't do yet
points: Checks prove the checks pass, not that the spec was right.
Still run by hand: interventions are recorded, fixes are manual.
One request at a time on the runner.
scenes.voice: Now, the limits. Checks prove the checks pass... not that the spec was right. That's exactly why a person approves the spec. The meta loop is still manual. The runner handles one request at a time. And it works best on small, clear requests.

scenes.title: Get a playground
scenes.say: Your own GitLab project, nothing to install. The code: github.com/sanjeev23oct/software-factory
scenes.voice: Want to try it yourself? There's a playground. Your own GitLab project, with nothing to install. File an issue, and watch it go through. The code is open source, and there's a longer write up on Medium.
